    #159946. The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1823 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • In a recent development, on November 10, The Fresh York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v.
    • According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    In a recent development, on November 10, The Fresh York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”.

    According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

    The Times story has reverberated swiftly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and vital source.

    Both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

    According to recent reports, as most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “remarked in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:.

    The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

    In fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

    In a recent development, scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

    Returning to Heller and the phrase at concern, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

    Rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”.

    Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

    Sources indicate that so how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam said that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

    (Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”).

    Industry observers note that from there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s Latest York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at glitch is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.).

    Sources indicate that this test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

    Industry observers note that this is particularly relevant since the court is currently preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

    The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more important problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

    Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The king tides caused major waves, but little more than minor flooding.
    • (CN) âÂ Several beaches along the coast of Southern California saw record high tides Wednesday, thanks to the convergence of three factors: the astronomical event known as “king tides,” the “El NiÃ±o” climate cycle, and global warming.
    • It has been revealed that preliminary data measured high tide at the Los Angeles Harbor, in the San Pedro neighborhood, at 8.19 feet, tying the previous record of about a month ago, with records going all the way back to 1923.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The king tides caused major waves, but little more than minor flooding.

    (CN) âÂ Several beaches along the coast of Southern California saw record high tides Wednesday, thanks to the convergence of three factors: the astronomical event known as “king tides,” the “El NiÃ±o” climate cycle, and global warming.

    It has been revealed that preliminary data measured high tide at the Los Angeles Harbor, in the San Pedro neighborhood, at 8.19 feet, tying the previous record of about a month ago, with records going all the way back to 1923. La Jolla and Santa Barbara had all-time record high tides, though the data for Santa Barbara only goes as far back as 1990.

    Recent findings suggest that state and local officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, had warned extensive flooding could disrupt travel plans and flood coastal communities. Those fears appear not to have been fully realized.

    Todd Hall, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service’s Los Angeles office in Oxnard, said two factors prevented the tides from being worse: Storm surge in Northern California petered out, and the high tide and large swells happened independently.

    “There is some reprieve, because the high tide this morning, surf and swell coming up into tonight,” Hall said. “Things would be much worse if we had high surf arriving at the same time we had high tide.”.

    Some areas did see minor flooding. Streets were underwater in the low-lying neighborhood of Sunset Beach in Huntington Beach this morning. Meanwhile, in the Bay Area, water from San Francisco Bay spilled onto the Embarcadero, and in Pacifica massive waves destroyed a section of the municipal pier. Santa Cruz County and Marin County both issued evacuation warnings for homes along the coast, though the latter has already been lifted.

    Warnings and advisories remain in place up and down the coast, but so far, the king tides have been less destructive than feared.

    Recent findings suggest that “It is a relief, that things weren’t worse,” said Febe Rothenberg, meteorologist at the National Weather Service in San Francisco. Still, she warned: “Pretty please, avoid the beach.”.

    King tides, also called perigean spring tides, are predictable astronomical events that occur when a fresh or full moon lines up with both the sun and Earth. The gravitational pull of the three bodies combine and cause exceptionally high tides. The next king tide will be a month from now, on Christmas Eve, when tides could be even higher if a storm hits.

    This year’s especially strong El NiÃ±o means unusually warm surface waters in the Pacific Ocean, with higher-than-average tides, larger waves and more frequent storms.

    Scientists predict tides will be higher and higher because of global warming, which has melted glaciers and caused ocean levels to rise 3-4 inches in the last 30 years.

    #159939. Moritz family to Ohio State law school: What’s going on with our $30M gift?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (243 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Moritz family to Ohio State law school: What’s going on with our $30M gift?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (243 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jeffrey Moritz has written in the Columbus Dispatch that his father’s $30 million donation to Ohio State University’s law school has inexplicably fallen and has only provided 12 to 15 scholarships each year.
    • When Michael Moritz donated more than $30 million to Ohio State University’s law school in 2001, he expected that the money would fund four faculty chairs and 30 annual law school scholarships.
    • But despite that agreement, records from the law school renamed after him show that the fund inexplicably fell from $30 million to $21.9 in less than 15 years, his son Jeffrey Mortiz writes in the Columbus Dispatch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jeffrey Moritz has written in the Columbus Dispatch that his father’s $30 million donation to Ohio State University’s law school has inexplicably fallen and has only provided 12 to 15 scholarships each year. (Image from Shutterstock).

    When Michael Moritz donated more than $30 million to Ohio State University’s law school in 2001, he expected that the money would fund four faculty chairs and 30 annual law school scholarships.

    But despite that agreement, records from the law school renamed after him show that the fund inexplicably fell from $30 million to $21.9 in less than 15 years, his son Jeffrey Mortiz writes in the Columbus Dispatch. Only 12 to 15 scholarships have been provided annually, he adds.

    Sources indicate that in the column, Moritz called upon the Ohio legislature to fix this by passing the Endowment Accountability Act, House Bill 751 and Senate Bill 368 by the end of December. The bill states that donors who believe a public university has violated an endowment agreement must first notify the state’s attorney general, who has 180 days to correct course. Donors in Ohio now have no clear way to hold public universities accountable.

    A former head of Baker & Hostetler’s corporate practice and director of Cardinal Health, Michael Moritz attended Ohio State’s law school on a full-ride scholarship before graduating in 1958. Less than a year after making his donation, Moritz, 68, was killed by a hit-and-run driver in Naples, Florida.

And âthere is always a strong public interest in the exercise of free speech rights otherwise abridged by an unconstitutionalâ government action.â.

    AliKhan rejected the governmentâs argument that the license renewal was inherently tied to an initial March 2025 anti-discrimination probe into Disneyâs hiring practices â part of the Justice Departmentâs ongoing campaign to roll back diversity, equity and inclusion practices â and the companyâs refusal to provide requested documents.

    âIf defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings to punish plaintiffs for their protected expression, then it is irrelevant whether defendants could conjure up an adequate basis to investigate plaintiffs or subsequently deny their licenses,â AliKhan wrote. âAs plaintiffs put it, they âdo not ask whether there was any violation of FCC rules,â but instead bring a textbook retaliation claim that is well suited for judicial resolution.â.

    Beth Wilkinson, of Wilkinson Stekloff and attorney for ABC News, described the FCCâs threats to a hanging guillotine, the falling of which would amount to a âcorporate death penalty.â.

    âAny broadcaster of ordinary firmness â wealthy or not â would not hesitate to think twice if faced with such an existential threat to its business,â AliKhan wrote, rejecting the Trump administrationâs assertion that the Disney Company could not be readily intimidated due to its wealth.

    The Justice Department argued the FCC was obligated to initiate the anti-discrimination investigation, as regulated entities and trustees of the nationâs public airwaves must serve the public interest.

    Industry observers note that at an Oct. 6 hearing, Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel highlighted President Donald Trumpâs July 16 national address from the White House, where he advanced baseless claims of election fraud, that ABC News and NBC News declined to broadcast as proof the outlet was not acting in the public interest.

    AliKhan further rejected the governmentâs argument that the broadcaster could only seek relief in the D.C. Circuit over concerns that any action taken by AliKhan would undermine her and the appellate courtâs jurisdictions. She noted that any such challenge would only come after an FCC denial, and if the FCC renews the licenses, then the broadcaster would have no First Amendment retaliation claim.

    The FCCâs license review of ABC News and eight of its regional affiliates â the stationâs licenses were set to expire between December 2028 and August 2031 â is the first use of the process in nearly 60 years, Wilkinson said.     ABC temporarily suspended Kimmelâs show for five days hours after Carr issued an ultimatum that âwe can do this the easy way or the hard way.â.

    • On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.
    • In a recent development, now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, last term in Little v. Hecox, which concerned whether states could bar transgender female athletes from participating in girl’s and women’s sports, Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked Idaho Solicitor General Alan Hurst: “Do you dispute that having a case named after you makes your infamy ... live forever? ...     On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.

    In a recent development, now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned. In this article, we offer a glimpse at the lives of a baker, a farmer, an executive director at Planned Parenthood, two students, and a leader of the Ku Klux Klan. But besides having interesting (and sometimes disturbing) life stories, what do they all have in common? Each asked the Supreme Court to answer one of the most fundamental questions of all: Where does government power end and personal liberty begin?

    Joseph Lochner: Lochner v. Newly introduced York.

    Let’s start with Joseph Lochner. Lochner immigrated from Bavaria, Germany, to the United States at the age of 20 in 1882, and settled in Utica, New York. He sought employment in the bakery industry; around 1890, he opened his own small, family bakeshop in Utica.

    Recent findings suggest that during this time, efforts emerged across Upcoming York to regulate the conditions of bakery workers after an article written by Edward Marshall, a muckraker, revealed their unsanitary conditions. In 1895, the state passed The Bakeshop Act, which aimed to prevent biscuit, cake, and bread bakers from working more than 10 hours a day or 60 hours a week.

    Twice charged with violating this statute, Lochner decided to challenge the law on the grounds that it violated the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause, which he argued protected the economic liberty to enter into such a contract with one’s employees.

    Lochner ultimately made its way to the Supreme Court and presented the court with the question of whether Fresh York’s law violated Lochner’s fundamental liberty interest. Everyone agreed that, under the powers reserved to the states, New York certainly had some powers to regulate general welfare. The question was whether New York had gone too far in restricting an employer’s freedom to contract with his employees.

    For some, the Fresh York statute was perfectly legitimate and a function of the democratic process. As then-future Judge Learned Hand argued, “we should not have the inconsistent spectacle of a government, in theory representative, which distrusted the courage and justice of its representatives, and put its faith in a [judiciary] which was, and ought to be, the least representative of popular feeling." Put simply, if there was a legitimate legislative purpose for the law, then according to Hand, courts should defer to what the elected representatives decided.

    According to recent reports, in what was seen even at the time as a surprising decision, the Supreme Court sided with Lochner five to four. “The general right to make a contract in relation to his business is part of the liberty of the individual protected by the Fourteenth Amendment of the Federal Constitution,” wrote Justice Rufus Peckham in his majority opinion.

    Sources indicate that while Peckham conceded there could be grounds for the legislature to implement regulations to improve workplace safety, he also held there was not sufficient evidence that the Bakeshop Act’s hour-limits would actually improve worker health. And if the statute was upheld, Peckham argued that it would open up almost every aspect of life to state regulation.

    In dissent, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes lampooned the majority, writing that “a constitution is not intended to embody a particular economic theory.”.

    Lochner has since been abandoned and its reasoning rejected by most legal scholars. Yet defenders remain. Law Professor Randy Barnett, for example, argues for a theory that if the government wants to institute a regulation of liberty, “the burden of proof is more or less on the legislature.” This gets at a fundamental debate in constitutional law: Why do certain civil liberties not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution get heightened scrutiny while economic liberty does not?

    As for Lochner himself, he returned to private life and continued to run his bakery. He died on December 14, 1939.

    It has been revealed that roscoe Filburn: Wickard v. Filburn.

    Industry observers note that few cases are more detested by constitutional conservatives than Wickard v. Filburn. Roscoe Curtiss Filburn was born on August 2, 1902, in Dayton, Ohio. A fifth-generation farmer, Filburn grew crops and raised livestock. The crops included winter wheat, which was, in part, for personal use.

    In a New Deal effort to help prop up the struggling agriculture industry, Congress enacted the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938. The secretary of Agriculture would create a national allotment of acres that could be used to produce wheat. The allotment would then be appropriated to states and ultimately to individual farmers. Filburn’s allotment in 1940 was for 11.1 acres of wheat, but he planted 23 acres of it. Administrators of the AAA fined Filburn 49 cents per excess bushel that he grew and placed a lien of $117.11 on his entire wheat yield.

    Filburn challenged the excess penalty in court on the grounds that the statute was passed under the Commerce Clause, which states that Congress shall have the power to “regulate Commerce ... among the several States.” Filburn contended that his activities did not implicate interstate commerce.

    If the winter wheat was grown by Filburn and never crossed state lines, could Congress then regulate it?

    The Supreme Court sided against Filburn, holding unanimously that his economic activities, taken in the aggregate, would have a substantial effect on interstate commerce. The logic went as follows: If Filburn grew his own wheat, then he would not need to purchase wheat on the open market; and if many farmers did this, it would undermine Congress’ efforts to stabilize the price of crops. “That [Filburn’s] own contribution to the demand for wheat may be trivial by itself is not enough to remove him from the scope of federal regulation where, as here, his contribution, taken together with that of many others similarly situated, is far from trivial,” explained Justice Robert Jackson.

    The decision remains controversial to this day (to put it mildly). Critics of Filburn argue that the decision gives Congress near unlimited power to enact regulations under the Commerce Clause, effectively allowing Congress to regulate every aspect of people’s lives and largely mooting the powers reserved to the states. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the Supreme Court appeared ready to reduce the Commerce Clause’s reach, striking down two statutes as exceeding Congress’ power. But it has not invalidated a law on these grounds since. (Although the Supreme Court in National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius held that Congress lacked the power to enact the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate under the Commerce Clause, it ultimately upheld the mandate under Congress’ power to tax.).

    Filburn returned to private life after his Supreme Court case and rarely spoke about it. During the 1950s, he purchased Beverly Shop, a woman’s beauty store, and, in 1966, Filburn convinced the other successors to his grandparent’s 640-acre farm to collectively sell the land to developers. He died on October 4, 1987, at the age of 85.

    Industry observers note that estelle Griswold: Griswold v. Connecticut.

    Estelle Griswold was born on June 8, 1900, in Hartford, Connecticut. A talented singer, she attended The Hartt School of Music, a music conservatory in Hartford. In 1935, she moved to Washington, D.C. for her husband’s job, where she volunteered at a doctor’s office and worked at George Washington University as a lab instructor.

    In the 1950s, Griswold moved to New Haven and a few years later was offered the role of executive director of the Planned Parenthood League of Connecticut. In 1961, she opened a birth control clinic in New Haven, along with a doctor, but was convicted and fined $100 in violation of the Barnum Act, a Connecticut law that prohibited the use of “any drug, medicine, article, or instrument” to prevent conception (and, yes, named after that Barnum).

    It has been revealed that griswold challenged her conviction on the grounds that the Barnum Act was unconstitutional. As some of the act’s legal defenders pointed out, although many may regard such a law as a profound violation of personal autonomy, the Constitution lacks any mention of “privacy,” never mind preventative contraception. Put succinctly by Justice Potter Stewart in his dissenting opinion, “I can find no such general right of privacy in the Bill of Rights, in any other part of the Constitution, or in any case ever before decided by this Court.” (To be fair, the idea of the Constitution containing a right to privacy was not upcoming when Griswold was decided; albeit in a different context, Justice Louis Brandeis had articulated such a right in an 1890 law review article.).

    In a 7-2 decision, the Supreme Court found the Barnum Act unconstitutional and held that married couples have a right to contraception as part of an implicit right to privacy. Justice William Douglas contended that the lack of its enumeration does not preclude that right from existing under the Constitution, akin to precedent in which the court found a parental right to send their children to religious schools. According to Douglas, “specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance. ... Various guarantees create zones of privacy.”.

    Sources indicate that while Douglas’ vote for a constitutional right to privacy won the day, his articulation of penumbras and emanations did not fare so well (although Justice Clarence Thomas apparently still pays “tribute” to this language with a sign in his office reading “Please do not emanate into the penumbra”). Rather, concurring in the judgement, Justice John Harlan II argued that the “teachings of history [and] solid recognition of the basic values that underlie our society” based in the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause supported the decision in Griswold, a standard that has since become the prevailing defense of the right to privacy and served as a foundation for later Supreme Court decisions such as Roe v. Wade and Obergefell v. Hodges.

    Soon after the decision was confirmed, the PPLC clinic reopened, but Griswold stepped down as executive director as she had fallen out of favor with some members of the organization due to its continued financial struggles. Griswold passed away on August 13, 1981, in Fort Myers, Florida at age 81 and was posthumously inducted into the Connecticut Women’s Hall of Fame in 1994.

    It has been revealed that the Tinkers: Tinker v. Des Moines.

    Another major area of constitutional controversy has involved the limits of free speech in the classroom context. Although such cases continue to crop up (BONG HiTS 4 JESUS, anyone?), the modern foundation for them was laid in 1969’s Tinker v. Des Moines. Which brings us to the Tinkers.

    According to recent reports, john Tinker was born in 1950, and his sister, Mary Beth, was born in 1952. They grew up in Atlantic, Iowa, where their father was the pastor of a Methodist church. In November 1965, John, then a high schooler, attended a rally in opposition to the Vietnam War in Washington, D.C. On the way back to Iowa, John and other protesters agreed to wear black armbands to protest the war and to mourn the deaths on both sides.

    Industry observers note that more than 50 students across public schools in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to school on December 16, 1965, in support of Sen. Robert Kennedy’s proposed Christmas truce. However, local principals instituted a policy that all students wearing black armbands would be asked to remove them.

    Recent findings suggest that on December 16, 1965, Mary Beth wore a black armband to Warren Harding Junior High School and was suspended after she refused to take it off. The next day, John wore a black armband to North High School and was also suspended after declining to remove it.

    In March 1966, the Tinkers sued, arguing the schools violated their constitutional rights. Specifically, the Tinkers contended that the public schools were an arm of the state and they were therefore bound by the First Amendment.

    Allan Herrick, arguing for Des Moines at the Supreme Court, contended that the school district must be in a position to “preserve order and to avoid this disturbance and disruption in the school room.” As Justice Thomas would argue decades later in Morse v. Frederick, “through the legal doctrine of in loco parentis [in the place of a parent], courts [historically] upheld the right of schools to discipline students, to enforce rules, and to maintain order.”.

    According to recent reports, in February 1969, the Supreme Court sided with the Tinkers, holding that students do not “shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.” In its decision, written by Justice Abe Fortas, the court established the substantial disruption test, which sets the necessary conditions for regulating student speech. To do so, the school must be able to reasonably foretell “material and substantial interference” with other students’ learning or the school’s operations. Fortas held that the school district failed to show that the Tinkers’ protests resulted in any material disruption.

    To this day, Tinker receives mixed reviews. Supporters of an expansive interpretation of the First Amendment tend to support the principles in Tinker and argue that they should be even more broadly applied; critics, such as Justice Thomas, are skeptical that students have First Amendment rights at all. (As Justice Hugo Black put it in his Tinker dissent, “It may be that the Nation has outworn the old-fashioned slogan that ‘children are to be seen, not heard,’ but one may, I hope, be permitted to harbor the thought that taxpayers send children to school on the premise that, at their age, they need to learn, not teach.”).

    In a recent development, after the Supreme Court’s decision, John Tinker remained active in anti-Vietnam war demonstrations and later became the manager of KPIP-LP 94.7 FM, a local radio station, which he manages to this day. Mary Beth Tinker pursued a career in medicine, working as a pediatric and emergency room nurse and a nurse practitioner. In 2013, Mary Beth left the nursing field and embarked on the “Tinker Tour,” where she travels the country telling her story and promoting civic education to young people.

    Recent findings suggest that clarence Brandenburg: Brandenburg v. Ohio.

    Let’s conclude with our least likable plaintiff, who nevertheless established one of the most enduring Supreme Court precedents. Clarence Brandenburg was born on March 3, 1916, in Lee County, Kentucky. A Marine Corps veteran, he worked at a General Electric plant and operated a television repair shop upon returning to civilian life. After declaring personal bankruptcy in 1959, Brandenburg began getting involved with white supremacist organizations and sought to become a leader of the KKK.

    In June 1964, Brandenburg spoke at a Klan rally, which was shown on a local television station. Brandenburg said “We're not a revengent organization, but if our President, our Congress, our Supreme Court, continues to suppress the white, Caucasian race, it's possible that there might have to be some revengeance taken. ... We are marching on Congress July the Fourth, four hundred thousand strong.” He was then charged with violating Ohio’s criminal syndicalism statute prohibiting advocating “sabotage, violence, or ... terrorism ... as a means of accomplishing ... political reform,” and later convicted.

    Industry observers note that brandenburg appealed, arguing that his speech was protected by the First Amendment. Specifically, he argued that Ohio could not punish him for advocating for unlawful action without showing that his speech was directed towards producing such action.

    Leonard Kirschner, arguing on behalf of Ohio at the Supreme Court, asserted that Brandenburg’s actions were not conducted in isolation and could lead to violence, contending that “the statements [made by Brandenburg] to 10 or 20 people can cause one heck of a lot of crime and violence and terrorism in any community. It only takes one person to cause it.”.

    The Supreme Court reversed Brandenburg’s conviction in 1969 on First Amendment grounds. According to the court, the Ohio statute in question failed to distinguish between an abstract endorsement of unlawful activity and speech directed towards producing imminent, lawless action. In doing so, the court established what became known as the Brandenburg test, which required that speech sufficient for incitement be “directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action” and “likely to incite or produce such action.”.

    Sources indicate that in 1971, Brandenburg was found guilty of harassing his Jewish neighbor by repeatedly calling him and uttering antisemitic slurs. He died on March 29, 1986.

    According to recent reports, they came from different backgrounds, had very different worldviews, and dealt with different issues, but each of these plaintiffs had one thing in common: pushing up against the limits of state power. How that power manifested itself differed considerably, as did the court’s willingness to reign it in. For example, while the court has advanced a highly protective understanding of the First Amendment, it has been more hesitant to advance protections of economic liberty.

    In a recent development, the nature of the plaintiff also mattered less in these cases than one might presume. Filburn was a farmer who grew wheat for his own personal consumption but did not prevail at the court. Brandenburg, on the other hand, expressed white supremacist ideas yet proved successful before the justices, becoming responsible for an entirely upcoming free speech doctrine.

    Some may view the court blinding itself to the actual facts on the ground as too simplistic; others as an ideal to aspire to. On that note, we’ll give Justice Elena Kagan the final word: “the question is not do you like this party or do you like that party ... the question is what the law requires.”.

    Blake Fox is an intern for SCOTUSblog.

    #159933. Breaking: Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2008 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that when the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court.
    • According to recent reports, four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners.
    • Sources indicate that the contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that when the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson to leave Cook in office while the case proceeded. Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett dissented. The administration lost, but the court’s disagreement did not reflect the familiar ideological split.

    According to recent reports, four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners. In Trump v. Kingdom, Thomas and Alito indicated that they would have granted the requested stay, but no other justice publicly held that position. Unlike Trump v. Cook, which produced a signed opinion after oral argument, the Kingdom order disclosed nothing about the reasoning or votes behind the court’s denial.

    Sources indicate that the contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief. And whereas some justices have supported federal executive positions at broadly similar rates across presidencies, others appear far more likely to do so depending on whether the president is a Republican or Democrat.

    According to recent reports, the prior article in this series examined how frequently the Trump and Biden administrations prevailed. In turning to the individual justices, I reviewed federal executive-action decisions from 2017 through November 12, 2026, consolidated into 106 distinct substantive decisions. The three administrations account for 32, 36, and 38 decisions, respectively.

    There is a very crucial qualification throughout: the court often publishes emergency orders without identifying each justice’s vote. The analysis thus assigned a justice to the court’s majority ruling when they were silent, absent an express position or other evidence indicating otherwise.

    So what can we say about the different justices’ support for the Trump administration on the emergency docket?

    Different presidents, different justices.

    Industry observers note that the most consistent record belongs to Roberts. He aligned with federal executive positions in 23 of 31 eligible decisions during Trump’s first administration, 26 of 36 under Biden, and 28 of 38 during Trump’s second administration. Those figures amount to 74%, 72%, and 74%. The disputes changed markedly, but Roberts’ aggregate willingness to leave the federal government’s position intact – or grant it relief – barely moved. In other words, Roberts has typically supported executive power on the emergency docket regardless of who is president.

    The next most consistent justice, Barrett (though with a much lower sample size), aligned with Biden in 69% of her eligible decisions and Trump II in 78%. Third was Kavanaugh, with rates of 78%, 67%, and 79%. Then came Gorsuch, with rates of 83%, 54%, and 84%.

    Thomas and Alito present a very different picture. Thomas supported the executive in 83% of eligible Trump I decisions, 39% under Biden, and 92% under Trump II. Alito’s corresponding figures were 83%, 47%, and 92%.

    The liberal justices show the opposite movement, although their individual records differ. Kagan supported executive positions in 43% of eligible Trump I decisions, 94% under Biden, and 24% under Trump II. Sotomayor’s rates were 27%, 94%, and 16%. Jackson, who joined the court during Biden’s presidency, supported its executive position in 21 of 24 eligible decisions (88%), compared with three of 38 (8%) under Trump II.

    The figure above makes these distinctions particularly clear. Roberts remains between 72% and 74% across the three periods, while Thomas’ support moves from 83% under Trump I to 39% under Biden and 92% under Trump II. The middle group of Barrett, Kavanaugh, and Gorsuch is more varied, but each supported Biden’s executive position more frequently than a simple Republican-versus-Democratic framing might suggest.

    Sources indicate that these numbers are telling, but they do not establish the reasons for why the justices decided as they did. For example, a president defending an environmental rule presents a very different legal issue from one seeking permission to remove an independent agency official. To determine how much of the observed variation is associated with presidential identity, the next step is to examine the kinds of cases that produced it.

    The issues that unite and divide the justices.

    It has been revealed that immigration provides a useful point of comparison because it generated substantial emergency litigation under all three administrations. Roberts supported the executive in 10 of 11 immigration decisions under Trump I, three of six under Biden, and 11 of 13 under Trump II. Thomas supported the government in 10 of 10 eligible Trump I immigration decisions, two of six under Biden, and 12 of 13 under Trump II. Kagan’s comparable figures were six of eleven, six of six, and five of 13.

    Industry observers note that this is revealing. Roberts and Thomas both supported Trump’s immigration positions at high rates but not as much when Biden defended his administration’s policies. Kagan and Sotomayor supported Biden in all six coded immigration decisions, then opposed most of Trump II positions. But there is, of course, a key caveat: This category covers different immigration rules, as opposed to simple support for one president over another.

    Public-health and related health litigation under Biden revealed a sharper division within the conservative majority. In 10 eligible health-coded decisions, Roberts and Kavanaugh each supported the federal executive in seven, compared with one each for Thomas and Alito. Barrett supported it in five; Gorsuch in two. Kagan and Sotomayor each supported the government in nine such cases. (Jackson’s two favorable positions came from only three eligible decisions in this category, making her figure much less informative.).

    It has been revealed that the court’s January 2022 vaccination decisions supply a concrete example. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in allowing the administration to enforce a vaccination requirement for workers at healthcare facilities receiving Medicare or Medicaid funding, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. On the same day, Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the conservatives in blocking OSHA’s broader vaccination-or-testing standard. To Roberts and Kavanaugh, health litigation was clearly treated issue-by-issue.

    Let’s move on to personnel decisions, or the president’s control over the executive branch. In the nine Trump II personnel and removal decisions, Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett supported the executive in eight, while Roberts and Kavanaugh did so in seven. In four foreign-affairs and national-security decisions, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch aligned with the government in all of these, compared with two for Roberts and Barrett.

    Subject matter therefore helps explain how things break down. The same conservative justice may support emergency intervention in a dispute over immigration enforcement while resisting it in a case involving agency regulation. The legal authority being asserted, the posture of the case, and the requested remedy all shape the decision.

    The coalitions inside the conservative majority.

    So which justices most frequently aligned? At the front of the pack are Thomas and Alito, who agreed in all 38 coded Trump II decisions. Their alignment is particularly visible when the administration lost. In seven events, both of their positions favored more relief for the administration than the majority granted or would otherwise provide.

    Recent findings suggest that other pairings are almost as cohesive. Roberts and Barrett agreed in 35 of 36 Trump II decisions (97%). Roberts and Kavanaugh agreed in 36 of 38 of these (95%), as did Gorsuch and Kavanaugh. The next figure displays those pairings alongside the liberal and cross-ideological relationships. The high agreement rates show how often the conservatives arrive at the same apparent disposition, but the exceptions reveal competing views about the scope of emergency judicial intervention.

    Recent findings suggest that the foreign-assistance dispute in Department of State v. AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, for instance, separated Roberts and Barrett from Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh. The four dissenters would have granted the administration relief from an order requiring payment for foreign-aid work already completed. Roberts and Barrett did not join that position. Their disagreement concerned what a district court could require of the government while the underlying funding litigation continued.

    According to recent reports, A different alignment emerged in NIH v. American Public Health Association. There, the court granted partial relief in litigation over terminated research grants. Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh would have granted the administration’s request in full, while Roberts joined Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson in seeking to deny it altogether. Barrett supported an intermediate outcome.

    It has been revealed that in Cook, the division shifted again. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in rejecting the administration’s attempt to immediately remove a Federal Reserve governor, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. In Trump v. Illinois, concerning the Trump administration’s deployment of National Guard forces, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch disagreed with the court’s denial of relief to Trump, while Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment on narrower grounds.

    The evidence points toward distinctive approaches to removal authority, spending, the judicial supervision of agencies, and emergency remedies. Justices who agree in one field can diverge in another, and partial orders sometimes put a justice between two groups seeking opposing forms of relief.

    The liberal justices and the unusual alliances across ideological lines.

    In a recent development, the three liberal justices also exhibited some meaningful disagreements. Under Trump II, Jackson aligned with the executive in only three of 38 emergency decisions (8%), compared with six for Sotomayor (16%) and nine for Kagan (24%). Kagan and Sotomayor agreed in 35 of 38 such decisions; Kagan and Jackson in 32. The differences are not as dramatic as those dividing the conservatives, but they complicate the assumption that the liberal trio behaves as a single bloc in every emergency dispute.

    Recent findings suggest that their publicly registered dissents differ as well. Jackson expressly opposed a Trump II executive position in 26 decisions, Sotomayor in 23, and Kagan in 20. In FCC v. Brown, for example, Sotomayor and Jackson publicly indicated that they would deny the agency’s stay application, while Kagan registered no public disagreement.

    Sources indicate that trump’s second term has produced more than one identifiable cross-ideological alignment. The five-justice majority in Cook included Roberts, Kavanaugh, and the three liberals, while the NIH grants dispute placed Roberts and the liberals together against complete relief. Barrett also joined certain portions of Sotomayor’s dissent in Trump v. J.G.G., a dispute involving the Alien Enemies Act, although her partial join should not necessarily be counted as agreement with the liberals on the case.

    These examples again highlight why the distinction between shared results and shared legal reasoning is important. A justice can favor the same outcome as an ideological opponent while arriving there for entirely different reasons (we see this with concurrences in merits cases all the time). Separate opinions can also reveal agreement on a particular procedural or statutory question even when the justices disagree on the ultimate relief. At the same time, the emergency docket makes these relationships especially difficult to measure comprehensively because many orders contain no individual vote information at all.

    My analysis of the emergency docket shows a chief most reluctant to favor one administration over another, with Barrett and Kavanaugh following closely behind; Gorsuch acting more favorably towards the Trump administration, although not overwhelmingly so; Thomas and Alito disproportionately favoring Trump over Biden; and the three liberal justices acting as a near mirror image of Thomas and Alito – although to varied degrees.

    We thus see a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.

    Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I dedicate my Thanksgiving column each year to the Indian Nation from whom I learned so much, the Tohono Oâodham, with whom I spent six of the best years of my life.

    In a recent development, I taught English, music and journalism and coached distance runners on the second-largest Indian reservation in the United States. The Oâodham are the only Indian Nation that never was at war with the United States and never were removed from their homelands.

    And I bet youâve never heard of them.

    The reason they never were at daggers drawn with Uncle Sam is that the Oâodham were a sedentary, transhumant agricultural tribe whose perennial enemies were the Apache.

    Transhumant means the quasi-sedentary people moved regularly from one climate zone to another, then returned: highlands in the summer, when itâs so hot on the desert floor, and you can hunt animals on the mountains, then back to the desert when the rains came, to harvest beans and squash.

    In Oâodham itâs called ak chin farming: farming at the mouth of the wash.

    A wash is a dry riverbed. You can see them all over what we call southern Arizona. The only time thereâs water in a wash is right after a monsoon rain. Mark Twain remarked he fell into a desert river once, âand came up all dusty.â.

    On the year I moved to the rez to teach at Baboquivari High School, I had an average of 43 students in my three English classes, and no desks for students, only the one for me.

    Fortunately, or not, it was the band room, so my students shared music stands to write out my assignments.

    Fortunately, or not, the ceiling was falling down, and, stashed in a closet, with a jumble of battered horns â all of our horns were battered â a kindly janitor had left us half a gallon of ceiling plaster. Which I used to patch up the pads on the flutes, saxophones and clarinets.

    Thatâs how it was on the rez when I got there. All but forgotten by Uncle Sam. And in some ways, good riddance to our uncle. But not so good that our uncle wouldnât buy desks for the only public school on the 3-million-acre reservation: twice the size of Delaware.

    Well, you do what you can, and you do what you must.

    Recent findings suggest that I dug life on the rez. Learning stuff I never knew I didnât know. Tryna pick up the language, and man, thatâs a tough language to learn. About all thatâs stuck with me is, âAyy, jum skug!â.

    Jum skug, as I understand it, means someone is âtrying to act.â Like a major shot.

    I tried not to be jum skug. Still try not to.

    I loved those years on the rez. Those 2,200 days.

    It has been revealed that hereâs another thing I learned. Iâll bet youâve been in this situation: Youâre in a party of mostly white people (mirgan); conversations are bubbling along in a crowded room, then all at once, the room is silent. Two, four seconds pass, then someone notes something, probably stupid, just to *break the silence.*People laugh, and the party continues.

    Itâs like the mirgan canât stand silence in a room.

    Recent findings suggest that iâve been in rooms with Oâodham where that silence continues, and no one feels that itâs necessary to break the silence. When someone finally speaks, itâs because sheâs got something to say â itâs not because she canât stand silence.

    Thereâs nothing wrong with silence.

    Here are some other things I learned on the rez.

    If you donât know what to say, shut up.

    If youâre not sure of what you want to say, shut up.

    If youâre called upon to speak, but donât know what you want to say, or donât know much about the subject: shut up.

    In celebration of Thanksgiving today (Thorâs Day), Iâd like to address all 535 members of Congress, and all of their appointed staffs, all the appointed members of the executive branch, and all the appointed, paid-off, cushy and cowardly members of our Supreme Court: to all of them, and to so many more, in our federal and state houses around the nation, Iâd like to tell yâall what I learned on the rez:.

    If you donât know what youâre talking about, shut the fuck up.

    (CN) â The Belgian region Wallonia said no to two wind turbines near its capital to protect the views, but the EUâs top court ruled Thursday that even scenery could take a back seat to qualifying renewable projects under the blocâs emergency rules.

    According to recent reports, eneco Wind Belgium asked the national Council of State to overturn the Walloon regionâs refusal to let it build and operate the turbines in Andoy, on the outskirts of Namur. The tech giant argued officials had overlooked the priority its project should receive underÂ an emergency EU rule. The Belgian judgesÂ asked the Court of Justice of the European Union how far that rule could go.

    Eneco filed for its permit in April 2023, a few months after the EU moved to speed up renewable energy construction. Russiaâs invasion of Ukraine and cuts in Russian gas supplies had sent energy prices soaring. Getting wind and other renewable projects online faster offered a way to replace some of that fuel.

    In Andoy, the plans called for access roads, a substation and underground cables. A public inquiry drew complaints, and Walloon officials turned down the project that October, citing the areaâs landscape and heritage. Officials reviewing Enecoâs appeal recommended a permit with conditions. The ministers handling the appeal missed the deadline to notify Eneco of a decision, so the refusal stood.

    It has been revealed that the EU judgesÂ saidÂ projects recognized as serving an overriding public interest had to get priority even when the competing concern fell outside EU rules on birds, habitats and waterways. Limiting that advantage to those environmental laws, they reasoned, would blunt a measure designed to speed up permitting.

    For Hendrik Schoukens, a professor of environmental law at Ghent University, the ruling narrowed officialsâ discretion in an area where governments set their own standards. âThis is vital, since landscape protection is not a harmonized interest by EU law,â he remarked.

    Sources indicate that officials could still put a competing interest first if they gave reasons specific to the project. The judges pointed to the ruleâs instruction to weigh those interests case by case. âThat provision would be devoid of purpose if the priority of those projects were to arise automatically from the mere recognition of their being of overriding public interest,â the court wrote.

    According to recent reports, for projects that needed an exception to EU bird or habitat protections, there was still the question of whether they could go ahead another way. Harm Dotinga, a senior legal adviser on nature protection at BirdLife Netherlands, stated a well-supported refusal could still protect biodiversity. He pointed to separate legal requirements, including the need to show there was no satisfactory alternative. âThose may also justify rejection of the project if properly motivated,â he said. Schoukens said it was striking how little attention the Belgian proceedings had paid to alternatives, given that a more sustainable option could still sink a project.

    In a recent development, whether a project qualified for priority in the first place depended on what stood in its way. Officials could rely on an existing presumption that it served an overriding public interest, including where national law extended that presumption to landscape protection. Where the presumption did not apply or was called into question, the project needed formal recognition.

    Sources indicate that eline Dhaen, a spokesperson for Eneco Belgium, stated the company was reviewing the ruling. The Walloon Region did not respond to a request for comment.

    A permit with conditions, as officials had recommended in Andoy, was another option. The court noted authorities could require developers to limit or make up for environmental damage and, where the law allowed, let some measures follow approval. Where species protection was at stake, the priority rule required conservation measures backed by sufficient funding and land.

    Elisa Cristea, a senior associate specializing in energy and environmental law at Romanian firm Èuca ZbÃ¢rcea & AsociaÈii, welcomed the ruling and saw conditional permits as its most practical point.

    âThis reflects a shift in the approach to permitting: Authorities should consider how competing interests can be accommodated rather than treating them solely as grounds for refusing a project,â she said.

    Sources indicate that cristea said the judges left officials more leeway than Advocate General Athanasios Rantos, who had proposed that departures from the priority rule be exceptional and backed by a detailed assessment. She said the ruling could outlast the expired emergency measure if EU lawmakers adoptedÂ a European Commission proposalÂ to restore priority over a wider range of competing interests.

    In a recent development, thursdayâs ruling is binding and cannot be appealed. Belgiumâs Council of State now has to apply it to the question still open in Andoy: whether Walloniaâs refusal stands.

    #159927. Protecting Attorney-Client Relationships: ABA advocacy helps safeguard the right to effective assistance of counsel

    📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (916 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Protecting Attorney-Client Relationships: ABA advocacy helps safeguard the right to effective assistance of counsel

    📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that attorney-client privilege, the lawyer’s ethical duty of confidentiality and the U.S.
    • To defend these principles and ensure lawyers can continue to represent their clients effectively, the ABA actively engages with Congress and federal agencies based on its long-standing policies passed by its House of Delegates.
    • In 2022 and 2024, the ABA helped defeat the Enablers Act, which would have harmed many lawyers and law firms by regulating them as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act and requiring them to report extensive attorney-client privileged and other protected client information to the government.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that attorney-client privilege, the lawyer’s ethical duty of confidentiality and the U.S. Constitution’s right to the effective assistance of counsel are bedrock legal principles that encourage clients to speak candidly with their lawyers without fear the information they share will be revealed to others. This enables clients to receive the most competent legal advice possible from fully informed counsel.

    To defend these principles and ensure lawyers can continue to represent their clients effectively, the ABA actively engages with Congress and federal agencies based on its long-standing policies passed by its House of Delegates. In the past decade, the association’s advocacy has resulted in significant successes, and the ABA continues to oppose various measures requiring lawyers to disclose protected client information. Recent examples illustrate the breadth of the ABA’s advocacy.

    In 2022 and 2024, the ABA helped defeat the Enablers Act, which would have harmed many lawyers and law firms by regulating them as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act and requiring them to report extensive attorney-client privileged and other protected client information to the government.

    The ABA also helped to reverse the “persuader” rule adopted by the Labor Department that would have required many lawyers and law firms representing employers to report confidential client information to the government. A federal court struck down the upcoming rule in 2016, and the Labor Department rescinded it two years later based in part on comments submitted by the ABA. The ABA continues to oppose legislative efforts to reinstate the rule, including the Protecting the Right to Organize Act of 2021, which has been reintroduced in each Congress since then.

    In a recent development, the ABA’s advocacy produced another notable result when U.S. Customs and Border Protection adopted a fresh policy in 2018 in response to concerns raised by the ABA. The new policy substantially increased protections for privileged and other confidential client information on lawyers’ laptops, cellphones and other electronic devices during border crossings.

    More recently, the ABA helped persuade the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to formally withdraw its proposed “duty of candor” rule, which would have imposed upcoming regulations on many lawyers representing clients before FERC and required them to disclose confidential client information to the agency. The ABA submitted comments to FERC in 2022 urging it not to apply the rule to lawyers representing clients because it would undermine the authority of the state supreme courts and weaken both the attorney-client privilege and the confidential lawyer-client relationship. In November 2025, FERC announced that based on the comments from the ABA and other stakeholders, it was withdrawing the proposal and terminating the rulemaking proceeding.

    In a recent development, the ABA is at the moment working with the Treasury Department in an attempt to persuade the Financial Action Task Force to prepare a favorable mutual evaluation report on the United States’ efforts to combat money laundering. The FATF, the global standard-setting body, is preparing the report to determine whether U.S. laws, regulations and other measures relating to its financial institutions, lawyers and law firms, and other key sectors comply with current FATF standards or whether new U.S. regulations are needed.

    According to recent reports, in March 2026, ABA representatives met with FATF evaluators at the Treasury Department’s request to explain recent efforts by the U.S. legal profession to combat money laundering. This included the ABA’s adoption and implementation of the 2023 amendments to Rule 1.16 of the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct concerning lawyers’ due diligence obligations.

    It has been revealed that the ABA is also urging Congress to promptly enact the Effective Assistance of Counsel in the Digital Era Act, which would protect the attorney-client privileged status of email communications between federally incarcerated people and their lawyers. Although U.S. mail, phone calls and in-person visits between lawyers and their incarcerated clients are shielded by attorney-client privilege, emails—the only rapid means for clients to reach their lawyers—are not. This is because the Federal Bureau of Prisons requires incarcerated people to waive the privilege in order to access the only available digital network.

    The EACDEA would protect the confidentiality of incarcerated people’s email communications and, thus, their Sixth Amendment right to the effective assistance of counsel by ending the BOP’s mandated waiver of the privilege. The bill would require the government to obtain a warrant before accessing incarcerated people’s emails with their lawyers.

    Recent findings suggest that support for the bill’s passage, which has bipartisan co-sponsors in the House and Senate, has been a featured issue at the annual ABA Day in Washington, D.C., fly-in event three times. The ABA continues to lobby for its passage. At the same time, the ABA is seeking a voluntary change to the BOP’s practice by working with the bill’s champions to include report language in the fiscal year 2027 appropriations process reflecting congressional disapproval of the BOP’s waiver requirement.

    As Congress and federal agencies continue to adopt or consider policies requiring disclosure of information protected by the attorney-client privilege or the lawyer’s duty of confidentiality, the ABA will remain vigilant in monitoring and opposing such measures. The association will also take all other steps necessary to safeguard the confidentiality protections essential to the effective assistance of counsel and the fair administration of justice.

    Sources indicate that this report is written by the ABA Governmental Affairs Office and discusses advocacy efforts by the ABA relating to challenges being addressed by Congress and the executive branch of the U.S. government. Follow @ABAGrassroots on social media.

    UK confirms EU deal has exit clause

    • (AFP) â A trade deal struck last week between Britain and the EU as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s reset with the bloc contains a termination clause, London confirmed Thursday.
    • It comes as the leaders of the right-wing opposition Conservative and Reform UK parties suggested they could seek to scrap the agreements if they defeat Labour at the next general election.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It includes a clause meaning that if one party ends the agreement within its first 10 years they would have to pay to rebuild the border checks infrastructure that the deal removes.

    (AFP) â A trade deal struck last week between Britain and the EU as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s reset with the bloc contains a termination clause, London confirmed Thursday.

    It comes as the leaders of the right-wing opposition Conservative and Reform UK parties suggested they could seek to scrap the agreements if they defeat Labour at the next general election.

    Burnham has reignited the Brexit wars that dominated political discourse following the narrow victory for the leave campaign during the 2016 referendum by suggesting Britain could apply to rejoin one day.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.K. premier and top EU officials signed three agreements in Brussels on Nov. 20 designed to improve post-Brexit ties in the short-term, kicking decisions on their long-term relationship down the road.

    They include the so-called sanitary and phytosanitary deal, which the British government says could add 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7 billion) to the country’s economy by slashing red tape on food and drink exports.

    It includes a clause meaning that if one party ends the agreement within its first 10 years they would have to pay to rebuild the border checks infrastructure that the deal removes.

    “That termination clause is a standard practice in international treaties, and this one applies equally to both sides, including the EU,” Burnham’s deputy spokesperson told reporters.

    Recent findings suggest that U.K. officials said an upfront sum for breaking the deal had not been stipulated.

    An EU diplomat told AFP that the reciprocal clause “provides stability for the agreement to deliver its benefits.”.

    Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform think tank, said it “makes sense” for the EU given the ongoing debate in Britain about its future relations with Brussels.

    “It’s an insurance policy,” he told AFP.

    Friday’s summit also agreed measures linking the two sides’ emissions-trading schemes and allowing young people to study and work across U.K.-EU borders.

    On Thursday, Burnham’s government formally introduced into Parliament the legislation required to implement the trade and electricity agreements.

    According to recent reports, lawmakers will get their first chance to debate them on Dec. 7, with a vote expected to follow, Labour confirmed Thursday.

    The EU Partnership Bill, which the government also refers to as the “Cutting Costs” bill, will almost certainly be approved by the lower House of Commons, where Labour holds a large majority.

    In a recent development, it will see the U.K. align with EU rules for sectors covered by the agreements, something known as dynamic alignment.

    It has been revealed that the U.K. government says linking the pair’s carbon markets would create the world’s largest connected carbon market and exempt 6.5 billion pounds’ ($8.1 billion) worth of British exports from EU carbon border taxes.

    London and Brussels have given themselves six more months to reach agreement on reduced university tuition fees for EU students in Britain, a key demand of the bloc.

    Having previously stated he would like to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime, Burnham has promised to lay out options that could range from leaving things as they are to entering the customs union or becoming a member again.

    Recent findings suggest that the prime minister has vowed to present his options to the public after a year of “informal brainstorming” with the EU. He said this week that rejoining without a referendum would be “unthinkable.”.

    Several former Conservative prime ministers, including Rishi Sunak, Boris Johnson, Theresa May and David Cameron, have warned against reopening a debate that deeply divided the country.

    Reform leader Nigel Farage stated this week he would “repeal” the reset deal while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Thursday she “does not support” what Burnham is doing.
